design_detail: One-year follow-up of the 150 participants of Morgan et al. (2009): five groups of 30 defined at baseline (frequent ketamine use, more than four times a week; infrequent use, less than four times a week but at least once a month; abstinent former use, at least 1 month; polydrug controls; controls not using illicit drugs). About 80% (119 by the text) were retested a mean of 366.6 (SD 92.11) days later with the same battery, using alternate versions for all tasks except the CANTAB tasks (p. 122). Groups kept their baseline labels although some participants' use changed. Analysed by 2 × 5 repeated-measures ANOVAs (time × group) with Bonferroni or corrected paired post hoc tests, and by correlations between change in self-reported ketamine amount and change in cognitive scores in the frequent group (p. 124).
can_establish: Whether the group differences seen at baseline in this sample were still present after a year, how scores changed within each group over the year against two control groups retested on the same schedule, and whether, within the frequent group, changes in self-reported amount went with changes in two CANTAB scores.
cannot_establish: That ketamine caused the group differences or the changes (there are no data from before use, education and premorbid IQ differ, use changed little over the year, and groups were not reclassified when people changed their use); whether impairments reverse after stopping, which the authors say these data cannot really address (p. 131); or anything about the people not retested, who include two members of the frequent group who died.

sample.recruitment: The 150 baseline participants of Morgan et al. (2009), first recruited from the unit's database by snowball sampling, re-contacted 12 months after their first session (p. 122). All were paid; the UCL Graduate School ethics committee approved the study (p. 122).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Baseline group definitions as above. Drug-using participants had to abstain from psychotropic drugs for at least 24 hours before testing; all had to have no history of head injury, psychiatric illness or organic brain damage and English as native language (p. 122). The exclusion of psychiatric illness does not appear in the baseline paper's description of the same sample.
sample.attrition: 80% retested: by the text 25 of 30 frequent, 27 infrequent, 24 abstinent, 23 polydrug and 20 non-drug (p. 122); Table 2 gives 25, 27, 23, 24 and 21 (p. 125), and the sex counts of Table 1 sum to 25, 26, 23, 24 and 21 (p. 124). Two members of the frequent group died during the year in what the authors call ketamine-related accidents (p. 132); other reasons for loss are not given, and completers are not compared with those lost. Analyses used fewer participants than were retested (error df of 108 in most cognitive analyses), without explanation.
sample.selection_effects: The same convenience sample as at baseline. Loss was largest in the non-drug controls (a third). The frequent group's completers had a much lower baseline depression score (BDI 7.08) than the whole frequent group in the baseline paper (11.48), which suggests that more depressed frequent participants may have been lost, unless one of the two papers is in error (see reporting issues).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported drug history at both sessions; urine samples analysed (Medscreen) and 3-cm hair samples (Trichotech) collected to verify reports and group membership (p. 123); the authors state that 24-hour abstinence could not be verified biologically (p. 132). Hair ketamine is given in ng/mg (the baseline paper gives ng/mm for the same samples). The adapted CAGE was used to assess ketamine dependence (p. 122).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported (Table 2, p. 125). Frequent group: 2.77 (2.42) g per occasion on 20.08 (7.41) days per month at baseline (n = 30) and 2.18 (1.82) g on 16.0 (10.01) days at follow-up (n = 25), with 22 of 25 still using at least monthly. Infrequent group: 1.26 (1.11) g on 3.37 (2.08) days, then 1.11 (1.06) g on 4.70 (6.48) days. Abstinent group at follow-up: 3 of 23 using at least monthly; group means 0.6 (0.71) g on 2.63 (5.91) days per month. Neither frequency nor amount changed significantly over time (p. 124). Years of regular use 6.67 (6.21), 4.69 (1.99) and 6.89 (2.39) (χ²(2) = 12.9, P = 0.002); adapted CAGE scores 3.12 (1.14), 1.76 (1.46) and 1.60 (1.10) (p. 124). Hair ketamine at baseline 295.90 (635.27), 21.82 (46.27) and 4.92 (16.32) ng/mg; at follow-up 241.50 (550.72), 48.43 (104.56) and 14.89 (63.17), and 1.63 (6.34) in the polydrug controls (p. 126). Route and purity not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Cannabis, ecstasy, cocaine and alcohol use by group and session are in Table 2 (p. 125). Cannabis use did not change; ecstasy frequency differed by group without post hoc differences; cocaine frequency and amount fell in all drug-using groups; alcohol frequency rose in the infrequent ketamine group (pp. 124, 126). At follow-up 2 of 21 non-drug controls reported regular cocaine use, and regular cannabis use among polydrug controls fell from 28 of 30 to 16 of 24 (Table 2). No drug was adjusted for; frequency of cannabis and cocaine use did not correlate with the key measures (p. 129).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 24 hours, self-reported, not verifiable by urine (p. 132); the experimenters judged that no one appeared intoxicated (p. 132). The text gives days since last ketamine use at follow-up as 2.2 (2.81), 11.03 (9.72) and 540.54 (691.19) for the frequent, infrequent and abstinent groups (p. 124), but Table 2 gives 35.44 (94.59), 26.46 (61.82) and 34.71 (50.49) days (p. 125).

comparison.controls: Polydrug controls (23 retested by the text) and non-drug controls (20), followed on the same schedule, so that practice and retest effects can be compared across groups (p. 122).
comparison.matching: Not matched on education or premorbid IQ (lower in the frequent group); polydrug controls were matched on other drug use at baseline, but their use fell over the year (Table 2).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No data from before ketamine use; family history of mental illness (reported at baseline in the 2009 paper) and childhood adversity are not used or adjusted for here.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Polydrug controls used cannabis, ecstasy, cocaine and alcohol; at follow-up ketamine was found in their hair (mean 1.63 ng/mg) although none reported using it, and 2 non-drug controls were using cocaine (pp. 125–126).

outcomes.instruments: The same battery at both sessions, all in drug-free sessions (pp. 123–124): CANTAB pattern recognition memory (percentage correct), spatial working memory (errors and strategy) and Stockings of Cambridge (problems solved in the minimum number of moves); a source memory task (recognition d′, bias C, source accuracy); prose recall (immediate and after about 10 minutes); letter and category fluency; spot-the-word. Self-reports: the short O-LIFE (total score), the Peters et al. Delusions Inventory (reported as the number of yes responses, Figure 1), the Dissociative Experiences Scale, the Beck Depression Inventory, the Spielberger trait anxiety scale, and a Life Events Scale (positive and negative events over the past year). Testing took 1.5 to 2 hours with two 10-minute breaks (p. 123).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard tasks and scales, without comparison with norms; the CAGE adapted for ketamine has no validation data in the paper. The CANTAB tasks had a single version, so practice effects apply to them, as the authors note for two of them (p. 131).
outcomes.operationalization: Persisting decrement means a main effect of group over both sessions; decline or improvement means a within-group paired test after a time × group interaction (or a trend); the dose–response for delusional ideation is an ordering of group means. No clinical threshold is applied.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Bonferroni post hoc tests and corrected paired t-tests within analyses; correlations at P < 0.01 with outliers beyond 3 SD removed (p. 124); no correction across the 17 outcome analyses.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; the drug history was taken at the start of each session (p. 123), so testers knew group membership.

analysis.effect_sizes: F tests without effect sizes or confidence intervals; group means and SDs by session in Tables 3–4 (pp. 127–128). Spatial working memory errors: group F(4,108) = 4.16, printed P = 0.04; strategy: time × group F(4,108) = 2.59, P = 0.041; Stockings: time F(1,108) = 9.73, P = 0.002, time × group F(4,108) = 2.14, P = 0.081; pattern recognition: group F printed as (1,108) = 4.429, P = 0.002; recognition d′ (covarying premorbid IQ): time F(1,108) = 14.14, P < 0.001, group F(4,108) = 2.42, P = 0.055; letter fluency: time × group F(4,108) = 2.84, P = 0.027; O-LIFE total: time × group F(4,105) = 5.60, P < 0.001; PDI: group F(4,108) = 4.16, printed P = 0.04; BDI: group × time F(4,110) = 2.97, P = 0.022; DES: group F(4,106) = 4.69, P = 0.002; negative life events: group F(4,104) = 4.30, P = 0.003 (pp. 126–129). Correlations in the frequent group: change in amount with change in SWM errors r = 0.623 (P = 0.004) and with change in pattern recognition r = −0.732 (P < 0.001) (p. 129). Editors' calculation from Table 3 (pooled SD; retested n by the text): frequent group against polydrug controls, SWM errors d ≈ 0.65 (95% CI 0.07 to 1.23) at baseline and 0.28 (−0.29 to 0.85) at follow-up; Stockings −1.08 (−1.68 to −0.47) and −0.20 (−0.76 to 0.37); against non-drug controls, pattern recognition −0.75 (−1.36 to −0.14) and −0.06 (−0.65 to 0.53). From the plotted points of Figure 2 (exact coordinates from the PDF's vector graphics), r ≈ 0.55 (22 points) and −0.55 (25 points) (see reporting issues).
analysis.covariates: Premorbid IQ for d′ only, because it was the only variable correlated with an outcome that showed group differences; time since first testing was checked and did not change the results, which are not reported (p. 124).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or pre-specified primary outcome is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Correlations were run only where clear group effects emerged, and only two are reported; the number run is not stated. No time × group result is reported for spatial working memory errors or pattern recognition, the two measures the abstract highlights. Hair results are given without statistical tests. The change scores used in Figure 2 are not tabulated, and their sign convention is not stated.
analysis.power: Not reported; the authors say the sample was too small for analyses of people who changed their use (pp. 130, 132).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Averaged over both sessions, the frequent group made more spatial working memory errors than every other group and recognised fewer patterns than the infrequent and ex-ketamine groups (no difference from either control group is reported); yet its mean errors fell from 29.58 to 19.92 and its pattern recognition rose from 83.68% to 89.04%, close to the controls' follow-up means (88.41% and 89.58%), changes for which no test over time is reported, and its strategy and Stockings scores improved to the other groups' levels. Within the frequent group, larger increases in self-reported amount per occasion went with worse changes on the two CANTAB scores. Delusional ideation (number of PDI items endorsed) and dissociation were highest in the frequent group across sessions; O-LIFE totals fell over the year in every group except the frequent group; depression scores rose in the frequent (7.08 to 10.67) and abstinent (4.96 to 9.00) groups. Use of ketamine changed little on average, while some people's use changed in both directions.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says cognitive deficits were observed mainly in the frequent group and that in this group increasing ketamine use over the year correlated with decreasing performance on spatial working memory and pattern recognition, and concludes that heavy use is harmful to aspects of cognition and psychological wellbeing and that health education campaigns are needed (p. 121). The Discussion speaks of persisting decrements on these tasks (p. 129), of a “purely chronic effect” (p. 131) and of “marked, profound cognitive impairments” (p. 132). The data show the frequent group's mean scores improving on both tasks over the year (changes the paper does not test) and, on pattern recognition, close to the controls' means at follow-up; the correlations are between change scores in about 22 to 25 people, are weaker in the plotted data than in the text, and come from a figure whose axis conventions cannot be read literally (see reporting issues). The authors attribute the improvements on two other tasks to practice and to the frequent group's poor baseline (p. 131) but do not apply the same reasoning to the tasks they call persisting. The delusional dose–response is an ordering of group means; the reported post hoc tests compare the ketamine groups only with the controls. The rise in depression is presented as possibly a consequence of the drug (p. 132), but the frequent group's completers started well below the baseline paper's value for the whole group, and the abstinent group started from the lowest score of all. The causal conclusion of harm rests on observational group differences that the authors themselves say could reflect pre-existing differences, polydrug use and differences between people who use daily or monthly (pp. 131–132).

timeline.event: Earlier 3-year follow-up by the same unit of 18 people who had cut down their ketamine use: category fluency no longer different from polydrug controls, prose recall lower and digit cancellation slower at both sessions

Baseline report on the same 150 participants: frequent use associated with poorer spatial working memory, planning, pattern recognition and word recognition and with higher delusional, dissociative and depressive scores

replication.where_it_stands: No independent longitudinal replication appears in the sources read for this card; later studies were not searched by this reader, so the status is provisional. The Tier B list for ketamine includes later cross-sectional cognition and imaging studies still to be appraised. Within this cohort, the baseline cognitive differences of the frequent group partly persisted when averaged over both sessions but narrowed or resolved at follow-up, while differences in delusional ideation and dissociation remained.

funding.funder: Grant to H.V.C. from the UK Economic and Social Research Council (RES-000-23-0945) (Acknowledgements, p. 132).
funding.affiliations_note: All authors at the Clinical Psychopharmacology Unit, University College London; the baseline paper, funded by the same grant number, names H.V.C. and C.J.A.M. as grant holders (Morgan et al., 2009, p. 86).

what_would_settle_it: A longer prospective cohort with more than two waves, exposure reclassified at each wave by hair analysis, change in performance analysed against change in use with baseline performance, education and premorbid ability adjusted for, enough people who start, increase, reduce and stop use, control of practice effects with alternate forms and retested comparison groups, and attrition reported by baseline characteristics.

domains.note: Education and premorbid IQ differ and are adjusted for only in the d′ analysis; other drug use changed differently between groups (alcohol rose in the infrequent group, polydrug controls' use fell); family history and childhood adversity are not considered.

Groups kept their baseline labels although 3 abstinent participants were using ketamine at least monthly at follow-up, some of the frequent group had not used for up to 340 days, polydrug controls had ketamine in their hair and two non-drug controls used cocaine; the change in self-reported amount drives the correlations; text and table contradict each other on abstinence at follow-up.
The same convenience sample as at baseline (database and snowball recruitment); losses after baseline are judged under missing data.
Whether anyone received treatment or changed circumstances in the year is not reported; changes in other drug use were large in some groups, and the frequent group reported more negative life events.

About 20% were not retested, up to a third of the non-drug controls, including two deaths in the frequent group; completers are not compared with those lost, and the BDI discrepancy with the baseline paper suggests that loss may be related to the outcome; analysed numbers are below those retested without explanation.

Testers were not blind to group; the CANTAB tasks had one version, so practice effects apply; symptom measures are self-reports, and O-LIFE scores fell steeply in all other groups, which the authors suggest may be a problem with repeated administration (p. 131).

Correlations were run only where group effects emerged and only two are reported; the same F and P are printed for two different analyses, and several F–P–df combinations do not match; post hoc tests follow non-significant omnibus tests; the plotted data do not reproduce the printed correlations; the abstract's emphasis on declining performance does not match the group means.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Retesting both control groups on the same schedule is a strength, and the follow-up shows which baseline differences were stable. But exposure was not reclassified when use changed, losses were not examined and may be related to outcomes, confounders other than premorbid IQ were not adjusted for, and the key correlations are not reproducible from the paper's own figure. The source may be cited for the group means and changes over the year as reported (with the frequent group's tested improvement on strategy and planning, and its untested mean gains on spatial working memory and pattern recognition, stated alongside its averaged differences), for the persistence of higher delusional ideation and dissociation in the frequent group, for the rise in depression scores in the frequent and abstinent groups with the baseline caveat, and for the two deaths as reported; it should not be cited as showing that ketamine use worsens cognition over a year, that impairments are profound, or that the associations are dose-dependent.

key_findings.finding: Of the 30 participants per group, 80% were re-assessed after a mean of 366.6 (SD 92.11) days: 25 in the frequent, 27 in the infrequent and 24 in the abstinent ketamine groups, 23 polydrug and 20 non-drug controls.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Participants and design, last paragraph
key_findings.note: Table 2 gives follow-up numbers of 25, 27, 23, 24 and 21 (p. 125), and the sex counts in Table 1 sum to 25, 26, 23, 24 and 21 (p. 124); see reporting issues. Reasons for loss are not given apart from two deaths (p. 132).

key_findings.finding: Two members of the frequent ketamine group were lost to follow-up because they died during the year in what the authors describe as ketamine-related accidents; no further details are given.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › The profile of a ketamine user, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The paragraph continues, in general terms, that high doses leave people unresponsive and vulnerable to physical dangers such as drowning or traffic; it does not say that these were the causes of the two deaths, nor how the deaths were ascertained or linked to ketamine. Two deaths among 30 people in a convenience sample are a count, not a mortality rate.

key_findings.finding: Ketamine use did not change significantly over the year (main effects of group only, frequency F(1,50) = 47.81, P < 0.001, and amount F(1,51) = 11.61, P = 0.001; no effect of time or interaction). The frequent group reported 2.77 (2.42) g on 20.08 (7.41) days per month at baseline (n = 30) and 2.18 (1.82) g on 16.0 (10.01) days at follow-up (n = 25), 22 of 25 still using at least monthly; the infrequent group 1.26 (1.11) g on 3.37 (2.08) days and 1.11 (1.06) g on 4.70 (6.48) days; at follow-up 3 of 23 in the abstinent group were using ketamine at least monthly (group means 0.6 (0.71) g on 2.63 (5.91) days per month).
key_findings.note: Groups were analysed under their baseline labels. The baseline figures differ from those printed for the same 30 frequent participants in Morgan et al. (2009, Table 2: 3.80 g on 20.13 days), and the bracketed ranges in Table 2 are incompatible with many of its SDs (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Years of regular ketamine use were 6.67 (6.21) in the frequent, 4.69 (1.99) in the infrequent and 6.89 (2.39) in the abstinent group (χ²(2) = 12.9, P = 0.002); scores on the CAGE adapted for ketamine dependence were 3.12 (1.14), 1.76 (1.46) and 1.60 (1.10).
key_findings.note: The CAGE was adapted for ketamine from an alcohol and drug screening instrument (p. 122); no cut-off or validation for ketamine is given. The same paragraph gives days since last use at follow-up that contradict Table 2 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Hair ketamine was 295.90 (635.27) ng/mg in the frequent, 21.82 (46.27) in the infrequent and 4.92 (16.32) in the abstinent group at baseline, and 241.50 (550.72), 48.43 (104.56) and 14.89 (63.17) at follow-up, with 1.63 (6.34) in the polydrug controls at follow-up; no statistical test is reported.
key_findings.note: The Discussion says hair concentrations doubled in the infrequent group (p. 130). The polydrug controls' positive mean implies ketamine use by at least one control, though none was reported (Table 2). The baseline paper reports different values in ng/mm for the same baseline (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Among those retested, groups did not differ in age or sex but differed in years of education (F(4,114) = 3.47, P = 0.01; frequent 12.2 (4.91) against 15.23 (2.67) infrequent and 15.24 (3.35) abstinent, P < 0.05) and spot-the-word score (F(4,114) = 2.95, P = 0.023; frequent 46.25 (3.56) against infrequent 51.54 (3.92), P < 0.05).

Cannabis use did not change; ecstasy frequency differed by group (F(3, 61) = 3.12, P = 0.033) without post hoc differences; cocaine frequency (F(1,64) = 8.53, P = 0.005) and amount (F(1,64) = 8.79, P = 0.004) fell in all drug-using groups; alcohol frequency changed differently by group (F(4,97) = 6.21, P < 0.001), rising in the infrequent ketamine group (P < 0.001), with a trend towards a fall in the abstinent group (P = 0.023).
key_findings.locator: Results › Other drug use (Table 2), 2nd paragraph (p. 124, continuing on p. 126) and 3rd paragraph (p. 126)
key_findings.note: Table 2 (p. 125): at follow-up 2 of 21 non-drug controls were using cocaine regularly, and regular cannabis use in the polydrug group fell from 28 of 30 to 16 of 24. The Discussion describes other drug use as relatively stable apart from cocaine (p. 130).

key_findings.finding: Spatial working memory errors showed a main effect of group (F(4,108) = 4.16, printed P = 0.04), the frequent group making more errors than all others (P < 0.05); its mean errors were 29.58 (19.93) at baseline and 19.92 (17.56) at follow-up, against 11.48 to 18.32 at baseline and 12.48 to 15.89 at follow-up in the other groups.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cognitive assessments (Table 3) › Spatial Working Memory task › Total number of errors (p. 126); Table 3 (p. 127)
key_findings.note: F(4,108) = 4.16 corresponds to P ≈ 0.004, and the same F and P are printed for the PDI (see reporting issues). No time × group result is reported for this measure. Editors' calculation from Table 3: frequent group against polydrug controls d ≈ 0.65 at baseline and 0.28 at follow-up.

key_findings.finding: Spatial working memory strategy showed a time × group interaction (F(4,108) = 2.59, P = 0.041) from a better (lower) strategy score at follow-up in the frequent group (31.63 (5.31) to 27.33 (6.33), P = 0.003). Stockings of Cambridge scores rose over time (F(1,108) = 9.73, P = 0.002), most clearly in the frequent group (7.67 (1.74) to 9.50 (1.89), P = 0.003; interaction trend F(4,108) = 2.14, P = 0.081), which reached the other groups' follow-up range (9.33 to 9.87).
key_findings.locator: Results › Cognitive assessments › Spatial Working Memory task › Strategy, and Stockings of Cambridge task (p. 126); Table 3 (p. 127)
key_findings.note: The authors attribute these improvements partly to practice on single-version tasks and to the frequent group's poorer baseline (p. 131). The paired test for the Stockings task follows an interaction that was only a trend.

key_findings.finding: Pattern recognition showed a main effect of group (printed F(1,108) = 4.429, P = 0.002), with poorer scores in the frequent group than in the infrequent and abstinent groups (P < 0.01); the frequent group's mean rose from 83.68% (10.27) to 89.04% (7.24), against 88.41% (9.69) in the polydrug and 89.58% (10.35) in the non-drug controls at follow-up.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cognitive assessments › Pattern recognition memory (p. 126); Table 3 (p. 127)
key_findings.note: No interaction result is reported. The text also describes the abstinent group's higher scores against both control groups as a trend at P < 0.05. Editors' calculation from Table 3: frequent group against non-drug controls d ≈ −0.75 at baseline and −0.06 at follow-up.

key_findings.finding: Prose recall was lower at follow-up overall (time F(1,113) = 6.26, P = 0.014), the fall after a delay being larger at follow-up (time × delay F(1,113) = 6.37, P = 0.013), with no group effects; the frequent group's delayed recall fell from 7.48 (2.36) to 5.84 (2.37) idea units. Recognition d′, adjusted for premorbid IQ, was lower at follow-up overall (F(1,108) = 14.14, P < 0.001), with a trend for a group effect (F(4,108) = 2.42, P = 0.055); post hoc tests are reported as showing the frequent group below the abstinent (P = 0.002) and polydrug groups (P = 0.003).
key_findings.locator: Results › Cognitive assessments › Prose recall and Source memory task › Recognition (p. 126); Table 3 (p. 127)
key_findings.note: The pairwise P values are inconsistent with the omnibus F (see reporting issues). The authors attribute the time effect on d′ to poorer performance of all groups, but in Table 3 the non-drug controls' d′ rose slightly (2.62 to 2.67) and the polydrug controls' immediate recall rose (8.10 to 8.42). Bias (C) was higher at follow-up (F(1,108) = 28.74, P < 0.001); the direction of change in source accuracy is unclear (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Letter fluency showed a time × group interaction (F(4,108) = 2.84, P = 0.027) and a main effect of time (F(1,108) = 6.83, P = 0.01), with lower scores at follow-up in the frequent (P = 0.046) and abstinent (P = 0.023) groups; category fluency showed a trend interaction (F(4,108) = 2.16, P = 0.078), with improvement in the infrequent group (P = 0.022).
key_findings.locator: Results › Fluency › Verbal fluency and Category fluency, 1st paragraphs
key_findings.note: Table 3 (p. 127): letter fluency also fell in the polydrug (17.33 to 15.25) and non-drug controls (16.32 to 14.53), by amounts similar to the abstinent group's (17.36 to 15.12); only the infrequent group rose (15.21 to 17.25).

key_findings.finding: O-LIFE totals fell over the year in all groups (time F(1,105) = 102.34, P < 0.001; infrequent, polydrug and non-drug P < 0.001, abstinent P = 0.014) except the frequent group (19.76 (7.15) to 18.62 (7.06)), giving a time × group interaction (F(4,105) = 5.60, P < 0.001); at baseline the frequent group's total was not the highest (infrequent 22.00, abstinent 21.14, polydrug 20.29, non-drug 18.10).
key_findings.locator: Results › Psychological wellbeing (Table 4) › O-LIFE, 1st paragraph; Table 4
key_findings.note: The authors suggest the fall in the other groups may reflect age, less cocaine use or a problem with repeated administration of the measure (p. 131).

key_findings.finding: Delusional ideation (number of PDI items endorsed) showed a main effect of group (F(4,108) = 4.16, printed P = 0.04): the frequent (P < 0.001), infrequent (P = 0.009) and abstinent (P = 0.016) groups scored above the non-drug controls, and the frequent group above the polydrug controls (P = 0.002); means at baseline and follow-up 8.39 (3.30) and 8.04 (4.24) frequent, 6.92 and 6.62 infrequent, 7.00 and 6.52 abstinent, 5.63 and 4.50 polydrug, 3.90 and 3.95 non-drug.
key_findings.locator: Results › Psychological wellbeing › PDI (Fig. 1), 1st paragraph, and Table 4 (p. 128); Figure 1 (p. 129)
key_findings.note: No comparison of the frequent group with the infrequent or abstinent groups is reported, although the abstract describes a dose–response with frequent scoring higher than both. The PDI is reported here as yes responses, not as the total score of the baseline paper.

key_findings.finding: Depression (BDI) showed a group × time interaction (F(4,110) = 2.97, P = 0.022), with increases in the frequent (7.08 (5.27) to 10.67 (7.99), P = 0.041) and abstinent groups (4.96 (3.52) to 9.00 (8.48), P = 0.013); the infrequent group's score fell (10.04 to 8.08).
key_findings.locator: Results › Psychological wellbeing › BDI, 1st paragraph; Table 4
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: the baseline paper gives the whole frequent group's BDI as 11.48 (8.17); a completers' mean of 7.08 implies a mean of about 33 in the 5 not retested, or an inconsistency between the papers. The abstinent group started from the lowest baseline score of all groups.

key_findings.finding: Dissociation (DES) showed a main effect of group (F(4,106) = 4.69, P = 0.002), higher in the frequent group than in the polydrug (P = 0.015) and non-drug controls (P = 0.009) (frequent 76.95 and 75.09 at baseline and follow-up, polydrug 48.17 and 41.74, non-drug 35.67 and 47.00); trait anxiety was lower at follow-up overall (time F(1,107) = 4.10, P = 0.045); the frequent group reported more negative life events over the year than the infrequent (P = 0.016), polydrug (P = 0.013) and non-drug groups (P = 0.006) (F(4,104) = 4.30, P = 0.003).
key_findings.locator: Table 4 and Results › Psychological wellbeing › STAI (p. 128, continuing on p. 129); DES and LES, 1st paragraphs (p. 129)
key_findings.note: The DES values are about a tenth of those printed for the same baseline in the 2009 paper (784 for the frequent group); the scoring is not described in either paper.

key_findings.finding: In the frequent group, change in self-reported amount of ketamine over the year correlated positively with change in spatial working memory errors (r = 0.623, P = 0.004) and negatively with change in pattern recognition percentage correct (r = −0.732, P < 0.001); cannabis and cocaine frequency did not correlate with the key cognitive or wellbeing measures.
key_findings.locator: Results › Correlations between change in amount of ketamine use and other measures in frequent users (Fig. 2), 1st paragraph (p. 129); Figure 2 (p. 130)
key_findings.note: The text says the current ketamine-using groups, the heading and the Figure 2 legend the frequent group. Editors' calculation from the exact coordinates of the plotted points in the PDF's vector graphics: r ≈ 0.55 (22 points) and −0.55 (25 points), and the sign conventions of the two panels differ (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: The authors found no improvement in the abstinent group's cognitive function with continuing abstinence and no deficits in that group against either control group at either session; they suggest it had already recovered, but state that these data cannot really speak to the question and call for prospective studies following people into abstinence.

The authors state that a year may have been too short to see progressive deficits or recovery, that few participants changed their use, that the sample was too small for analyses of people who moved between groups, that 24-hour abstinence could not be verified biologically, and that the ketamine groups differed in education and premorbid IQ.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Methodological considerations, 1st paragraph (p. 131, continuing on p. 132)

reporting_issues.issue: Follow-up group sizes differ between the text (25, 27, 24, 23 and 20 for the frequent, infrequent, abstinent, polydrug and non-drug groups; p. 122), Table 2 (25, 27, 23, 24 and 21; p. 125) and the sex counts of Table 1 (25, 26, 23, 24 and 21; p. 124); the error degrees of freedom are 114 in the demographic analyses, 108 in most cognitive analyses and 104 to 113 elsewhere, and no account of missing data is given (editors' calculation: these df imply that 109 to 119 participants were analysed).
reporting_issues.consequence: The analysed numbers per group, and therefore the attrition by group, cannot be stated with certainty.

reporting_issues.issue: The same result, F(4,108) = 4.16, P = 0.04, is printed for two different analyses, spatial working memory errors (p. 126) and the PDI (p. 128); moreover, F(4,108) = 4.16 corresponds to P ≈ 0.004 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one of the two analyses carries the other's statistic; the size of both group effects is uncertain as printed, though either P would be below 0.05.

reporting_issues.issue: The main effect of group for pattern recognition is printed as F(1,108) = 4.429, P = 0.002 (p. 126); a main effect across five groups has 4 numerator degrees of freedom (editors' calculation: F(4,108) = 4.43 gives P ≈ 0.002, whereas F(1,108) = 4.43 would give P ≈ 0.04).
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a typing error in the degrees of freedom; the printed P fits the five-group test.

reporting_issues.issue: Post hoc results are reported after omnibus tests that were not significant: the frequent group below the abstinent (P = 0.002) and polydrug (P = 0.003) groups for recognition d′ after a group effect with P = 0.055; the frequent group's Stockings improvement (P = 0.003) after an interaction with P = 0.081; and the infrequent group's category fluency gain (P = 0.022) after an interaction with P = 0.078 (pp. 126, 128). Editors' calculation for d′ (F ≥ t²/4 for any pairwise comparison): if, as the Method states for main effects of group (p. 124), the post hoc P values are Bonferroni-adjusted, P = 0.002 implies an omnibus F(4,108) of about 3.7, far above the printed 2.42; if they are unadjusted, a P of 0.0020 to 0.0025 printed as 0.002 implies about 2.40 to 2.51, only marginally compatible with 2.42.
reporting_issues.consequence: The d′ post hoc values cannot all be right if they are Bonferroni-adjusted as the Method states, and are at most marginally compatible if they are not; claims that the frequent group's word recognition differed from other groups at follow-up should not rest on them.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the duration of abstinence at follow-up as 2.2 (2.81), 11.03 (9.72) and 540.54 (691.19) days for the frequent, infrequent and abstinent groups (p. 124), but Table 2 gives 35.44 (94.59), 26.46 (61.82) and 34.71 (50.49) days since last use at follow-up, with ranges up to 340 days in the frequent group and 0 to 140 days in the abstinent group (p. 125); the text's first two values resemble the table's baseline values (2 (2.60) and 11.30 (9.36)).
reporting_issues.consequence: Abstinence at follow-up cannot be established. If the table row covers the whole abstinent group, as its label says, every member of that group had used ketamine within 140 days of follow-up, and some of the frequent group had stopped, yet groups were analysed under their baseline labels.

reporting_issues.issue: Many bracketed ranges in Table 2 cannot be ranges for the SDs printed beside them (for example 20.08 ± 7.41 with range 17–23; 3.37 ± 2.08 with 3–4; 5.68 ± 14.52 with 0–14), one range runs backwards (0.39–0.072 g), and one includes 32 days in a month (p. 125).
reporting_issues.consequence: The bracketed values are probably intervals of another kind mislabelled as ranges; they should not be cited as ranges.

reporting_issues.issue: The Table 3 row labelled proportion of source memory errors falls from 0.85–0.89 at baseline to 0.68–0.79 at follow-up in every group (p. 127), while the text says all groups had a greater proportion correct at follow-up (p. 126); the baseline values match the proportion correct reported for the same measure in the 2009 paper (0.84 to 0.90; Morgan et al., 2009, Table 5, p. 83).
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the row label or the text is wrong, so the direction of the change in source memory over the year is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: The two panels of Figure 2 (p. 130) use opposite sign conventions. Editors' analysis of the plotted points (exact coordinates from the PDF's vector graphics): the x-values of panel A, labelled change in spatial working memory errors, average about +12 errors, whereas Table 3 (p. 127) shows the frequent group's mean errors falling by 9.7; and the y-values of panel A, change in ketamine use, reappear with reversed sign among the y-values of panel B (for example +4, +4 and +3.5 in A, −4, −4 and −3.5 in B). The most consistent reading is that panel A plots baseline minus follow-up on both axes and panel B follow-up minus baseline.
reporting_issues.consequence: If both axes of panel A are reversed, the sign of its correlation and the direction stated in the text are preserved, but panel A's axis labels cannot be read literally; the direction of the association rests on the text, and a second reader should check this reading.

reporting_issues.issue: The correlations printed in the text (r = 0.623, P = 0.004; r = −0.732, P < 0.001; p. 129) are not reproduced by the points plotted in Figure 2 (p. 130). Editors' calculation from the exact coordinates in the PDF's vector graphics: panel A has 22 points with r ≈ 0.55 (P ≈ 0.008); panel B has 25 points (three pairs coincide) with r ≈ −0.55 (P ≈ 0.004); least-squares lines through these points coincide with the lines drawn. No plotted point lies beyond 3 SD, so the stated removal of outliers (p. 124) cannot explain the difference; omitting any single point gives r between 0.45 and 0.69 in panel A and between −0.46 and −0.65 in panel B.
reporting_issues.consequence: The strength of the association between change in use and change in performance is overstated in the text and abstract, or the figure shows different data from those analysed; the spatial working memory correlation from the plotted points barely meets the paper's own P < 0.01 threshold.

reporting_issues.issue: For the same baseline participants, several figures differ from those in Morgan et al. (2009): the frequent group's amount per session (2.77 vs 3.80 g) and the SD of its frequency (7.41 vs 2.36 days per month), with n = 30 in both; hair ketamine at baseline (295.90, 21.82 and 4.92 ng/mg here; 282.14, 18.01 and 3.55 ng/mm there); the DES, about a tenth of the earlier values (frequent group 76.95 vs 784); the PDI, reported here as yes responses (8.39) rather than the earlier total score (22.72); and the frequent group's days since last use at the first session, 2 (SD 2.60) here against 1.6 (SD 1.27), range 1–7, there (pp. 125–128; Morgan et al., 2009, pp. 81, 84).
reporting_issues.consequence: Baseline values cannot be taken interchangeably from the two papers, and the two hair measures carry different units; each paper's own figures should be cited with their source.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstinent group's follow-up category fluency SD is printed as 0.98, against 3.36 to 5.82 in every other cell of that row (Table 3, p. 127).
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a typing error; this cell should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The Introduction describes ketamine as an NMDA receptor antagonist with the word ecstasy inserted in the parenthesis (p. 121). The published erratum (Addiction 105(4), p. 766; doi 10.1111/j.1360-0443.2010.02984.x; first published 10 March 2010), read on the publisher's page, states that including ecstasy in this description was incorrect, and corrects nothing else.
reporting_issues.consequence: None for the data. The PDF on file is the uncorrected original; every number on this card is as printed in it, and none is affected by the erratum.

verification.source_read: PDF PDFs/Ketamine/Morgan_2010_OneYearLongitudinal.pdf, printed pp. 121–133 (all 13 pages; Tables 1–4 checked on the rendered pages, the landscape Tables 2–4 on rotated 220-dpi renderings; Figure 2 point coordinates taken from the PDF's vector drawing objects). Erratum read in the app's browser on the publisher's page, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1360-0443.2010.02984.x (Addiction 105(4), p. 766): it corrects only the Introduction's description of ketamine, which wrongly included the word ecstasy (p. 121), and changes no numbers; all numbers on this card are as printed in the uncorrected PDF and are unaffected.

disagreements.first_pass: Post hoc results are reported after omnibus tests that were not significant: the frequent group below the abstinent (P = 0.002) and polydrug (P = 0.003) groups for recognition d′ after a group effect with P = 0.055; the frequent group's Stockings improvement (P = 0.003) after an interaction with P = 0.081; and the infrequent group's category fluency gain (P = 0.022) after an interaction with P = 0.078 (pp. 126, 128). Editors' calculation: for d′, a pairwise test with P = 0.002 on 108 df implies an omnibus F(4,108) of at least 2.5 (F ≥ t²/4), above the printed 2.42. | The d′ post hoc values cannot all be right; claims that the frequent group's word recognition differed from other groups at follow-up should not rest on them.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 228, corrected: the inference that the d′ post hoc values cannot all be right holds only if the printed P = 0.002 is Bonferroni-adjusted (as the Method states for main effects of group) or, if unadjusted, below about 0.0023; an unadjusted P of 0.0024–0.0025 printed as 0.002 is compatible with F(4,108) = 2.42 (P = 0.053).
disagreements.resolution: Recomputed: on 108 df an unadjusted two-tailed P of 0.002 gives t²/4 = 2.51 and 0.0025 gives 2.40; a Bonferroni-adjusted 0.002 (unadjusted 0.0002) gives 3.71. Issue and consequence reworded as conditional on the adjustment.

disagreements.first_pass: (with the frequent group's improvement on spatial working memory, pattern recognition, strategy and planning stated alongside its averaged differences)
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 228, missed: for spatial working-memory errors and pattern recognition only main effects of group are reported, with no time or time × group result, so the frequent group's mean changes are not shown to be reliable; the only tested within-group gains are strategy (P = 0.003) and Stockings (P = 0.003); 'mean change, not tested' would be more accurate for the first two.
disagreements.resolution: Verified on p. 126 (Results › Cognitive assessments). The description of what may be cited corrected; the domain judgments and the overall judgment are unchanged.

disagreements.first_pass: Averaged over both sessions, the frequent group made more spatial working memory errors and recognised fewer patterns than other groups; ... | The data show the frequent group improving on both tasks over the year and, on pattern recognition, not differing from the controls at follow-up;
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 228 (interpretation gap: agree, substantial), two precisions: 'recognised fewer patterns than other groups' should read 'than the infrequent and ex-ketamine groups' (p. 126; no significant difference from either control group); the frequent group's 'improving on both tasks' describes untested mean changes.
disagreements.resolution: Verified on p. 126. Both phrases corrected (no follow-up test against the controls is reported either, so 'not differing' became 'close to the controls' means'); the rating (substantial) is unchanged.
